items.prompt: Jordan signs in as HR at 09:00 with an eight-hour JWT; an Admin demotes Jordan at 09:10. What does Jordan's next request see, and why?
items.answer: The demotion, because each request reloads session, account and role from the DB
distractors: Full HR access until 17:00, because the role is signed into the eight-hour JWT
A 401 on every request, because any role change revokes all of Jordan's tokens
HR access until Jordan reloads the browser page and the client fetches a new token
items.explanation: The token carries stable account/session identity; authorization reads current state, so the next request observes the change. Logout deletes the server session too.

items.prompt: An HR user edits an employee and includes accountRole in the request body. What happens?
items.answer: Rejected, as HR cannot set account roles in employee requests
distractors: Applied, since HR manages all ordinary employee data
Ignored silently, and every remaining field is saved
Queued as a pending role change for an Admin to approve later
items.explanation: A business title (JobRole) is not a security role. Only Admin creates or changes accounts; HR also cannot edit an Admin employee.

items.prompt: A directory refresh is in flight when the user signs out; its authorized response arrives afterwards. How does the UI stop it restoring stale state?
items.answer: Sign-out bumps the request generation and clears caches, so old reads are ignored
distractors: Clearing the token is enough: the late response cannot be parsed without it
The fetch is aborted on sign-out, so its response is dropped by the browser
The server rejects the late response, as its session was deleted at logout
items.explanation: An old refresh may already hold an authorized response; the browser regression holds one, signs out, then releases it to prove the signed-out screen stays.

items.prompt: Why does Nethris open an immediate SQLite write transaction before reading the PTO balance it will change?
items.answer: It reserves the write lock before reading, so concurrent approvers take turns
distractors: Immediate transactions skip the WAL file, which makes each approval run faster
It lets EF SaveChanges commit every write as soon as that write is made
It lets other readers see the uncommitted balance deduction early
items.explanation: With an outer transaction, SaveChanges is not the final commit; the API owns one durable outcome for state, hours and history.

items.prompt: Maya's PUT carries the ETag for version 4, but Jordan already saved version 5. Why must the browser not just fetch the new ETag and resend Maya's draft automatically?
items.answer: It would silently overwrite Jordan's change instead of letting Maya review it
distractors: The server would reject the resend, because the operation key was already used
Strong ETags cannot be refreshed while an unsaved draft exists in the editor
It would lose Maya's draft, as the draft lives inside the old ETag value
items.explanation: A version protects intent. After review the user may keep the draft and retry with the latest version; the server stays authoritative.

items.prompt: A client reuses an operation key but sends a different body. What does Nethris return?
items.answer: A conflict, because the fingerprint stored for that key differs from this body
distractors: The recorded result of the first request, since the operation key matches
A fresh execution of the new body, stored under that same operation key again
A 428, because the If-Match header must change whenever the body changes
items.explanation: Same key plus same fingerprint replays the recorded result; same key plus different content is a conflict. Receipts are scoped to account and key, kept 24 hours.

items.prompt: What distinct problems do record versions and operation receipts solve?
items.answer: Versions detect stale intent; receipts recover one intent's outcome
distractors: Both prevent duplicates; a receipt is just the HTTP name for a version
Versions recover lost responses; receipts detect concurrent edits
Receipts replace versions entirely once idempotency keys are enabled
items.explanation: They are complementary: a stale edit is detected by the version; a lost response is recovered by replaying the same key.

items.prompt: PTO hours are stored as quarter-hour integers. A 120-hour balance has a 7.75-hour request deducted. What is stored, and what happens to a 0.1-hour request?
distractors: 112 units; 0.1 hours is rounded up to one quarter-hour
11225 units; 0.1 hours is stored as zero units
449 units; 0.1 hours is rounded down to zero and accepted
items.explanation: 120 h = 480 units, 7.75 h = 31 units, 480 - 31 = 449. Values that are not whole quarter-hours are refused instead of rounded silently.

items.prompt: When composing an EF expiry query, why does the guide capture 'now' into a local variable first?
items.answer: Putting UtcNow inside the provider expression caused a real setup failure
distractors: UtcNow is evaluated once per row, which makes the expiry query slow on big tables
SQLite stores local time, so UtcNow must be converted before comparing
A local variable is what lets the test suite freeze the clock
items.explanation: Timestamps are integer Unix milliseconds; translating UtcNow inside the expression failed during development.

items.prompt: When computing available PTO, how should pending and approved hours be treated?
items.answer: Pending hours reserve balance, and approved hours already reduced it
distractors: Subtract both pending and approved hours from the current balance
Ignore pending hours until the manager has approved them
Subtract approved hours only, since pending ones may still be rejected
items.explanation: Double subtraction is the trap; the rules are simplified teaching policy.

items.prompt: An update arrives with a well-formed strong ETag for the right record but an old version. Another arrives with no If-Match at all. Which statuses do they get?
items.answer: 409 for the old version, 428 for the missing header
distractors: 428 for both, as neither matches the stored row
409 for both, as both fail the concurrency check
412 for the old version, 400 for the missing header
items.explanation: HrisRequest.Expected only checks that the client stated a version for this record in the right form (428 otherwise); the comparison with the stored row happens later in HrisRules.Version (409).

items.prompt: In the red-first lab, disabling each guard (UUID key check, 428 guard, audit-log role minimum, logout session deletion) turns exactly one test red. What is the review finding?
items.answer: Each guarantee rests on a single test, so losing that test loses the protection
distractors: The suite is over-tested: a red test per guard is redundant coverage
The guards are unnecessary, as only one test notices each one missing
The tests are flaky, as a real regression should fail many tests at once
items.explanation: The table shows thin coverage: e.g. AuditLogs has no role check of its own, so MinimumRole and its one test are the only gate.

items.prompt: Adding a status filter, why parse with Enum.TryParse(..., ignoreCase: false, out value) AND Enum.IsDefined(value)?
items.answer: TryParse alone takes numeric strings like "7" that are not defined statuses
distractors: IsDefined makes the name comparison case-insensitive for the filter
TryParse throws on unknown names, and IsDefined catches that exception for it
IsDefined is needed so EF Core can translate the enum filter to SQL
items.explanation: An unparseable value must throw HrisError.Invalid (422) rather than being ignored, mirroring the departmentId block.

items.prompt: Where must the new status filter be applied relative to CountAsync and the page query?
items.answer: Into the one IQueryable that feeds both the count and the page
distractors: In React, after the page of employees has arrived from the API
Only into the page query, keeping the unfiltered total for the pager
After Skip and Take, so that the database has less work to do
items.explanation: If total comes from a differently filtered query, the pagination lies - and nothing in a screenshot shows it. Changing the filter should also reset offset to zero.

items.front: Password change revokes the current session in the same transaction. Why can't the client simply replay its receipt after a lost response, and what simple flow is acceptable?
items.back: The revoked session can no longer authenticate the replay. A documented flow: sign in again with the new password, and if that fails (outcome uncertain) with the old one. Do not promise ordinary receipt replay unless the design supports it.

items.front: Refunds: how should two different operation keys competing for one refund differ from a retry of the same key?
items.back: Different keys: one wins, the other observes the closed state or a uniqueness constraint. Same key: recover the already committed result. A version protects stale intent but does not replace refund uniqueness.

items.front: Stale-edit review: what state do you need to tell 'fields the other writer changed' from 'fields I changed'?
items.back: Three values per field: the snapshot the editor opened with, the draft, and the latest saved row. A field conflicts only when both sides moved away from the snapshot - so keep the opening snapshot in its own state.

items.front: Why does HrisRules.OptionalText map whitespace-only input to null instead of using input.Description?.Trim()?
items.back: So 'absent' has exactly one representation in the database. Trim() would store "" for a blank form, a second way to mean 'no description'; delegating to Text keeps the length rule in one place.
